newsitem.title: EGYPT: No breakthroughs in Egypt-Israel peace summit.
newsitem.headline: No breakthroughs in Egypt-Israel peace summit.

text.p: A summit in Egypt to revive the Middle East peace process ended on Tuesday without any breakthroughs, but it gave hope further talks would help overcome differences over Jewish settlement of Arab land.
Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak met Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in the Egyptian Red Sea resort of Sharm el-Sheikh to try and break the impasse in the peace process.
Mubarak said they discussed the controversial issue of settlements but both said any solution needed more talks.

"We exchanged views concerning the settlements and we are still going to have more discussions so as to put the key in the door and open it," Mubarak told a news conference in which the two men joked and appeared relaxed. "We need another meeting and we need more deliberation."

Asked if the further deliberations would include the Palestinians, Mubarak said: "We intend as far as we can to bring the main partner in(to) the meeting but this depends on so many elements. We hope that we could conclude it in the next meeting and then after that the third element could come."

A senior Israeli official said Mubarak's adviser Osama al-Baz will shuttle between the Israelis and Palestinians. He said Netanyahu felt at the end of the visit that the Egyptian effort was genuine and that Cairo could play a positive role.
"(The summit) was a gamble of sorts but for now the signs are positive. It was a first step," he said.
But an aide to Palestinian President Yasser Arafat said the meeting had not eased the crisis.
Peace talks halted in March when Netanyahu approved building a new Jewish settlement in Arab East Jerusalem. The Palestinians refuse to talk peace unless Israel stops the project.
Netanyahu referred to the meeting with Mubarak as a "positive beginning. But we need more work and we are committed to work together with you (Egypt) to achieve progress".
"This was a first step and a first step means there are more steps," Netanyahu said. "In no circumstances would I characterise what went on here today as a failure."
Some analysts had described the Sharm el-Sheikh meeting as crucial for deciding the fate of the peace process but others predicted it would not yield breakthroughs.
Mubarak has suggested Israel halt work on the Jerusalem settlement, known as Har Homa and Jabal Abu Ghneim, for six months to give the peace process new momentum.
Netanyahu, who has refused freezing settlements, did not reject the suggestion.
"I am not going to address myself to all sorts of things that appear in the press. I prefer to spend the coming time on concrete discussions with private channels," he said.
Egyptian Foreign Minister Amr Moussa had said he hoped Netanyahu would change his mind about settlements in Jerusalem, but the Israeli prime minister put a damper on that.
"We don't make a distinction between Jerusalem and communities we build outside Jerusalem," he said when asked about taking unilateral action in the city.

"But in general we believe Jerusalem to be an open city secure for all three faiths and our policy is also to ensure that we respect the needs and the rights of all of Jerusalem's residents, Jews and Arabs alike," Netanyahu added.
The Palestinians regard Israeli settlement building in East Jerusalem as pre-empting final status talks on the city, which they see as the capital of a future state.
